title: Ferromagnets and Electromagnets
lead: The magnets of the last section were taken as they came: a bar of iron with a pole at each end, and nothing said about where those poles came from. This section says which materials can carry them, how the small regions inside such a material called domains grow and line up to magnetize it, and why heating it above a certain temperature undoes that alignment altogether. It then makes a magnet out of nothing but a current in a coil of wire, which is what an electromagnet is, and it ends on the sentence the rest of the chapter is built on: electric current is the source of all magnetism.
objectives: Describe the role of magnetic domains in magnetization.
Explain the significance of the Curie temperature.
Describe the relationship between electricity and magnetism.
summary_html:
• Magnetic poles always occur in pairs of north and south—it is not possible to isolate north and south poles.
  • All magnetism is created by electric current.
  • Ferromagnetic materials, such as iron, are those that exhibit strong magnetic effects.
  • The atoms in ferromagnetic materials act like small magnets (due to currents within the atoms) and can be aligned, usually in millimeter-sized regions called domains.
  • Domains can grow and align on a larger scale, producing permanent magnets. Such a material is magnetized, or induced to be magnetic.
  • Above a material’s Curie temperature, thermal agitation destroys the alignment of atoms, and ferromagnetism disappears.
  • Electromagnets employ electric currents to make magnetic fields, often aided by induced fields in ferromagnetic materials.

figures.original_caption: An unmagnetized piece of iron is placed between two magnets, heated, and then cooled, or simply tapped when cold. The iron becomes a permanent magnet with the poles aligned as shown: its south pole is adjacent to the north pole of the original magnet, and its north pole is adjacent to the south pole of the original magnet. Note that there are attractive forces between the magnets.

(a) An unmagnetized piece of iron (or other ferromagnetic material) has randomly oriented domains. (b) When magnetized by an external field, the domains show greater alignment, and some grow at the expense of others. Individual atoms are aligned within domains; each atom acts like a tiny bar magnet.
An electromagnet with a ferromagnetic core can produce very strong magnetic effects. Alignment of domains in the core produces a magnet, the poles of which are aligned with the electromagnet.

An electromagnet induces regions of permanent magnetism on a floppy disk coated with a ferromagnetic material. The information stored here is digital (a region is either magnetic or not); in other applications, it can be analog (with a varying strength), such as on audiotapes.

(a) In the planetary model of the atom, an electron orbits a nucleus, forming a closed-current loop and producing a magnetic field with a north pole and a south pole. (b) Electrons have spin and can be crudely pictured as rotating charge, forming a current that produces a magnetic field with a north pole and a south pole. Neither the planetary model nor the image of a spinning electron is completely consistent with modern physics. However, they do provide a useful way of understanding phenomena.

exercises.prompt: A bar magnet is oriented so that the north pole of the bar magnet points north. A compass needle is placed to the north of the bar magnet. In which direction does the north pole of the compass needle point?

answer.hint: The compass needle sits beyond the north pole of the bar magnet, so ask which way the field of that magnet runs at a point out in front of its north pole, and remember that the north-seeking end of the needle turns to follow it.

exercises.prompt: Assume for simplicity that the Earth’s magnetic north pole is at the same location as its geographic north pole. If you are in an airplane flying due west along the equator, as you cross the prime meridian (0° longitude) facing west and look down at a compass you are carrying, you see that the compass needle is perpendicular to your direction of motion, and the north pole of the needle dipole points to your right. As you continue flying due west, describe how and why the orientation of the needle will (or will not) change.

answer.solution: The needle keeps pointing the same way relative to the airplane, so nothing about the picture in front of you changes as you fly. The north pole of the needle turns toward the end of Earth’s magnet that lies at the geographic north pole, and along the equator that direction is geographic north everywhere. Flying due west, north is always to your right, so the needle stays perpendicular to your direction of motion with its north pole to your right the whole way round. What does change is your heading in the fixed frame of the stars, since flying due west carries you round the equator, but the compass turns with you and reports the same relation between your motion and the field at every longitude. The needle would only swing if you left the equator, where the field begins to dip out of the horizontal, or if the magnetic pole and the geographic pole were not in the same place, which is the simplification the question grants.

exercises.prompt: Describe how the magnetic domains in an unmagnetized iron rod will respond to the presence of a strong external magnetic field.

options: The domains will split into monopoles.
The domains will tend to align with the external field.
The domains will tend to orient themselves perpendicular to the external field.
The domains will tend to align so as to cancel out the external field.
answer.hint: A domain behaves like a small bar magnet, and a small bar magnet free to turn in a field settles with its north pole along the field rather than across it; the domains already lying that way also grow at the expense of the rest.

exercises.prompt: Describe what steps must be undertaken in order to convert an unmagnetized iron rod into a permanently magnetized state. As part of your answer, explain what a magnetic domain is and how it responds to the steps described.

answer.solution: A magnetic domain is a region inside the iron, often about a millimeter across, in which the poles of the individual atoms all point the same way, so that the region behaves like one small bar magnet. In an unmagnetized rod the domains are small and point every which way, and their fields cancel, so the rod as a whole shows no poles. To magnetize it permanently, lay the rod in a strong external magnetic field, which is most simply done by placing it between two magnets or inside a current-carrying coil. The domains already lying along the field grow at the expense of their neighbors, and the neighbors that are left swing into line, so the rod becomes magnetized while the field is applied. To make that state stay when the field is taken away, either heat the rod and then let it cool while it lies in the field, or tap it with hard blows while it lies cold in the field. Both of these give the domain walls the chance to settle into the new arrangement rather than springing back, and the rod is then a permanent magnet with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. The heating must stop short of the Curie temperature of iron, 1043 K, because above that temperature thermal motion is too violent for any field to hold the domains in line at all.

exercises.prompt:
Iron is ferromagnetic and lead is diamagnetic, which means its magnetic domains respond in the opposite direction of ferromagnets but many orders of magnitude more weakly. The two blocks are placed in a magnetic field that points to the right. Which of the following best represents the orientations of the dipoles when the field is present?
IronLead
(a)dipoles pointing every which waydipoles pointing every which way
(b)dipoles all pointing to the rightdipoles pointing every which way
(c)dipoles pointing every which waydipoles all pointing to the right
(d)dipoles all pointing to the rightdipoles all pointing to the right

options: The dipoles of the iron and the dipoles of the lead both point every which way.
The dipoles of the iron all point to the right, and the dipoles of the lead point every which way.
The dipoles of the iron point every which way, and the dipoles of the lead all point to the right.
The dipoles of the iron and the dipoles of the lead both point to the right.
answer.hint: Iron is ferromagnetic, so its domains line up strongly along the applied field. Lead responds the other way and many orders of magnitude more weakly, so on this scale its dipoles are left looking as disordered as they were.

exercises.prompt: A weather vane is some sort of directional arrow parallel to the ground that may rotate freely in a horizontal plane. A typical weather vane has a large cross-sectional area perpendicular to the direction the arrow is pointing, like a “One Way” street sign. The purpose of the weather vane is to indicate the direction of the wind. As wind blows past the weather vane, it tends to orient the arrow in the same direction as the wind. Consider a weather vane’s response to a strong wind. Explain how this is both similar to and different from a magnetic domain’s response to an external magnetic field. How does each affect its surroundings?

answer.solution: The two are alike in the way they turn. Each is free to rotate, each is acted on by something that fills the space around it, and each settles pointing along that something: the vane lines up with the wind, and the domain lines up with the external magnetic field. In both cases a stronger wind or a stronger field brings the turning about faster and holds it more firmly against whatever tends to disturb it. They differ in three ways. The vane is one object that merely turns, whereas a domain is a region of the material whose boundary can move, so a domain lying along the field grows at the expense of its neighbors as well as turning; nothing about a weather vane grows. The vane's alignment is lost as soon as the wind drops, while a domain's alignment can be made to stay after the field is taken away, if the iron is heated and cooled or tapped while it lies in the field, which is how a permanent magnet is made. And thermal motion is nothing to a vane, while above the Curie temperature it is enough to keep the domains from lining up at all. They also differ in their effect on their surroundings. The vane takes a little momentum from the air and disturbs the wind hardly at all, so a second vane beside the first feels the same wind as before. The domain is itself a small magnet, so once it is aligned it adds its own field to the external one, and the sum of all the aligned domains is what makes the iron a magnet that pulls on other things and that can align its neighbors in turn.
